variants.angle: is level 10 fair or just mean
variants.title: I made a small puzzle game where pebbles sink after one hop. Level 10 keeps fooling my friends, is it fair or just mean?
variants.body: Solo dev here. Every pebble sinks once you leave it, so the whole puzzle is picking an order. Level 10 is where most of my friends restart a few times. I can't tell anymore if it's a good 'aha' or just unfair, so I'd love blunt opinions.
variants.first_comment: It's on the App Store if you want to try it: https://apps.apple.com/app/id0000000000. Tell me where you got stuck.

variants.title: My own puzzle game still beats me on level 10, and I'm the one who wrote the solver
variants.body: The solver says 8 hops. My record is 11. Here's the clip of the solver doing it like it's nothing.
variants.first_comment: App Store link, if you want to beat my 11: https://apps.apple.com/app/id0000000000

variants.title: Level 1 vs level 10 in my pebble-hopping puzzle: where does it stop feeling fair?
variants.body: Level 1 teaches that a pebble sinks after you leave it. By level 10 you have to plan the whole route before the first hop. I'm tuning the curve and would like to hear where it starts to feel like guessing.
variants.first_comment: Link for anyone who wants to try it: https://apps.apple.com/app/id0000000000

variants.hook:
Level 10 is the level I almost deleted.
Playtesters restarted it more than any other, and I read that as a bug.
variants.body:
It wasn't. They restarted because they could see the right route, just not in time.

So instead of making it easier, I made the mistake easier to see: the pebble wobbles before it sinks.

Restarts stayed about the same. Quits dropped.

Hard is fine. Unclear is what makes people leave.
variants.cta: How do you tell 'hard' from 'unfair' when you test your own work?
variants.first_comment: The game, if you want to try level 10 yourself: https://apps.apple.com/app/id0000000000

claims.text: restarted it more than any other

variants.angle: a solver that proves every level
variants.hook:
Before I ship a level, a solver has to beat it.
That one rule changed how I design puzzles.
variants.body:
The game is Flutter with a single CustomPainter, and the rules are plain Dart with no UI. That split means the same code runs the game, the tests and a breadth-first solver.

The solver finds the shortest route and that becomes the par. If it can't find one, the level doesn't ship.

It also caught three levels that had a shortcut I never saw.
variants.cta: Do you keep your game rules free of the UI layer? What did it buy you?
variants.first_comment: Clip is the solver's route through level 10. Game: https://apps.apple.com/app/id0000000000

claims.text: three levels that had a shortcut

variants.angle: solo dev beaten by own level
variants.hook:
I'm a solo dev and my own level 10 beats me.
Here's why I left it that way.
variants.body:
When you build a puzzle you know the answer, so you can't feel the difficulty anymore.

Watching other people play is the only honest test. Their restarts told me where the 'aha' was. My own playthroughs told me nothing.
variants.cta: What's your way of seeing your own work with fresh eyes?

I wrote a solver to prove every level of my puzzle game can be beaten.
It says level 10 takes 8 hops. My friends say it's impossible. 🧵 #PebbleHop #indiedev
thread: The rules are plain Dart with no Flutter imports, so the game, the tests and the solver share one copy of the rules.
Breadth-first search over (frog position, sunk pebbles). The shortest route becomes the par. No route, no ship.
It also found three shortcuts I never intended. Two stayed in. They were fun.
